A homotopy type $X$ is **locally finite** if every homotopy group $\pi_i(X,x)$ is finite for every point $x$, and for each $x$ there is an integer $n_x$ such that $\pi_i(X,x)=0$ for $i>n_x$.

Write $\pi_0(X)$ for the set of connected components. Let $\mathbb Q_c(X)$ be the rational-valued functions on $\pi_0(X)$ with finite support. For a component $x$, the **homotopy weight** is
$$
w_X(x):=\prod_{i>0}|\pi_i(X,x)|^{(-1)^i}.
$$
The product is finite because the positive homotopy groups vanish in high degrees; a negative exponent means a reciprocal.

For a map $f:X\to Y$ of locally finite homotopy types and $\alpha\in\mathbb Q_c(X)$, define
$$
f_!(\alpha)(y):=\sum_{x\in\pi_0(F_y)}\alpha(i_y(x))\,w_{F_y}(x),
$$
where $F_y$ is the homotopy fiber of $f$ at $y$ ([[def-homotopy-fiber-of-a-map]]) and $i_y:F_y\to X$ is its natural map. For a proper map, meaning one whose homotopy fibers have finitely many connected components, also define $f^*:\mathbb Q_c(Y)\to\mathbb Q_c(X)$ by $f^*\beta=\beta\circ\pi_0(f)$.

The ratio lemma [[lem-homotopy-fiber-component-weight-ratio]] proves that fibers of maps between locally finite homotopy types are locally finite and that the displayed sum is finite. The set of components of a homotopy fiber alone does not determine $f_!$.

Since $u$ is proper, this fiber has finitely many components; therefore $u'$ is proper on components.

Fix $y'\in\pi_0(Y')$ and put $y=u(y')$. The homotopy fiber of $f'$ over $y'$ is equivalent to the homotopy fiber of $f$ over $y$, with its map to $X$ equal to the composite of the fiber map to $X'$ and $u'$. Fix a finite field $k=\mathbb F_q$ ([[def-finite-field-and-its-order]]). Its field operations make it a commutative ring with unit by [[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]; this is the base ring for all DGA and dg-module structures below. A **small $k$-linear dg-category** $\mathcal T$ has a set of objects, a cochain complex $\mathcal T(a,b)$ of $k$-vector spaces for every ordered pair, closed degree-zero identity maps, and associative degree-zero composition chain maps
$$ \mathcal T(b,c)\otimes_k\mathcal T(a,b)\longrightarrow\mathcal T(a,c). $$
The cohomological grading and differential follow [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. For cochain complexes U,V use the direct-sum total tensor complex
$$ (U\otimes_k V)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}U^p\otimes_k V^q,\qquad d_{U\otimes V}(f\otimes g)=d_U f\otimes g+(-1)^p f\otimes d_Vg \quad(f\in U^p,\ g\in V^q). $$
The formula is k-balanced and additive because the two differentials are k-linear; extend it linearly from homogeneous tensors. It has degree $+1$ and squares to zero: on $f\otimes g$ its two mixed terms have coefficients $(-1)^{p+1}$ and $(-1)^p$, which cancel, and the remaining terms contain $d_U^2f$ or $d_V^2g$. Every element has finite support in the displayed direct sum, so this construction imposes no boundedness on U,V.

Writing $fg=f\circ g$ for $f\in\mathcal T(b,c)^p$ and $g\in\mathcal T(a,b)^q$, the requirement that composition commute with these differentials says exactly
$$ d(fg)=(df)g+(-1)^p f(dg). $$
Thus each endomorphism complex is a cohomological DGA in the sense of [[def-differential-graded-algebra]]: its multiplication is associative, unital and k-bilinear by the dg-category axioms, the scalar map is $\lambda\mapsto\lambda1_a$ and is central since $(\lambda1_a)f=\lambda f=f(\lambda1_a)$, and the displayed formula is precisely the DGA Leibniz rule. The identity has degree zero and is closed, as required above.

The dg-category is **locally finite** when, for every $a,b$, the graded vector space $\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i(\mathcal T(a,b))$ is finite-dimensional. Thus the cohomology is finite-dimensional and vanishes outside a finite set of degrees; no uniform bound over all pairs is assumed.

A **right dg $\mathcal T$-module** is a dg-functor $\mathcal T^{op}\to\mathrm{Ch}(k)$: it assigns a cochain complex $M(a)$ to each object and compatible degree-zero right composition actions. Explicitly, the right action is a degree-zero chain map
$$ M(b)\otimes_k\mathcal T(a,b)\longrightarrow M(a),\qquad m\otimes f\longmapsto mf, $$
with the tensor differential just fixed. For homogeneous $m\in M(b)^q$ and $f\in\mathcal T(a,b)^p$, its chain-map identity is
$$ d_M(mf)=d_M(m)f+(-1)^q m\,d_{\mathcal T}(f). $$
The actions are unital and compatible with composition. In particular, on each endomorphism algebra $\mathcal T(a,a)$ they give exactly the right differential graded module structure of [[def-differential-graded-module]], with the sign determined by the degree of m, not of f. No left action or ungraded identification with a left module is inferred. For $h_b=\mathcal T(-,b)$ the action is composition, so the composition identity above verifies this same right-module differential rule. A quasi-isomorphism is a module map inducing an isomorphism on every cohomology group at every object.

The enhancement used here includes the standard projective model category of right dg modules ([[def-model-category-and-quillen-adjunction]]): its weak equivalences are the quasi-isomorphisms just defined, its fibrations are objectwise degreewise surjections, and its representable modules are homotopically projective, so their dg Hom complexes compute derived Hom. Its homotopy category $\mathcal D(\mathcal T)$ is triangulated. The same objectwise homotopy theory is used for arrow diagrams and composable-pair diagrams. It is stable: it is pointed, and a square is a homotopy pushout exactly when it is a homotopy pullback. The translation is the cohomological shift, and a homotopy cofiber of a module map is represented functorially by its mapping cone. These homotopy-theory structures are part of the supplied dg enhancement; an unenhanced triangulated category alone is not an input.

For modules $a,b$, write $\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal T}(a,b)$ for the derived Hom complex in the supplied projective homotopy theory. Its derived mapping space has $\pi_j\operatorname{Map}(a,b)=H^{-j}\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathcal T}(a,b)=\operatorname{Ext}^{-j}_{\mathcal T}(a,b)$ for $j\ge0$. In the core homotopy type of a category of modules, $\pi_1$ at $a$ is $\operatorname{Aut}(a)$ and $\pi_i=\operatorname{Ext}^{1-i}_{\mathcal T}(a,a)$ for $i>1$.

For $a\in\mathcal T$, the **representable right module** is $h_a=\mathcal T(-,a)$. A module is **perfect** if its object in $\mathcal D(\mathcal T)$ belongs to the smallest full triangulated subcategory containing all representables and closed under retracts. This means it is obtained from finitely many representables by finite direct sums, shifts, cones, and direct summands. For perfect modules set
$$ \operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal T}(x,y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D(\mathcal T)}(x,y[i]). $$

For a triangulated category $T$ with shift $[1]$, a **t-structure** is a pair of strictly full subcategories $(T^{\leq0},T^{\geq0})$ such that $T^{\leq0}[1]\subseteq T^{\leq0}$, $T^{\geq0}[-1]\subseteq T^{\geq0}$, $\operatorname{Hom}_T(T^{\leq0},T^{\geq1})=0$, and every $X$ has a distinguished triangle $A\to X\to B\to A[1]$ with $A\in T^{\leq0}$ and $B\in T^{\geq1}$. Here $T^{\geq1}=T^{\geq0}[-1]$ and $T^{\leq n}=T^{\leq0}[-n]$, $T^{\geq n}=T^{\geq0}[-n]$. Its **heart** is $T^{\leq0}\cap T^{\geq0}$.

For the triangulation of [[thm-the-derived-category-inherits-a-triangulated-structure]], the canonical candidate is $D^{\leq0}=\{X:H^i(X)=0\text{ for }i>0\}$ and $D^{\geq0}=\{X:H^i(X)=0\text{ for }i<0\}$, using [[prop-cohomology-factors-through-the-derived-category]].

Let $(\mathcal T^{\le0},\mathcal T^{\ge0})$ be a t-structure on a triangulated category $\mathcal T$ with translation $[1]$ ([[def-canonical-t-structure-on-a-derived-category]], [[def-triangulated-category]]), and set $\mathcal T^{\le n}:=\mathcal T^{\le0}[-n]$ and $\mathcal T^{\ge n}:=\mathcal T^{\ge0}[-n]$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$; thus $X\in\mathcal T^{\le n}$ exactly when $X[n]\in\mathcal T^{\le0}$, and $X\in\mathcal T^{\ge n}$ exactly when $X[n]\in\mathcal T^{\ge0}$.

For $X\in\mathcal T$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$, the t-structure axiom applied to the translate $X[n]$ and then shifted by $[-n]$ produces a distinguished triangle
$$\tau_{\le n}X\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow\tau_{\ge n+1}X\longrightarrow\tau_{\le n}X[1]$$
with $\tau_{\le n}X\in\mathcal T^{\le n}$ and $\tau_{\ge n+1}X\in\mathcal T^{\ge n+1}$; such a triangle is a **truncation triangle** of $X$ at $n$. Truncation triangles of the same $X$ at the same $n$ are canonically isomorphic over $X$, so the objects and maps occurring in them are determined up to a unique compatible isomorphism ([[lem-truncation-triangles-are-essentially-unique-and-functorial]]); one writes $\tau_{\le n}$ and $\tau_{\ge n}$ for the resulting **truncation functors**.

The **t-cohomology** of $X$ is
$$H^n_t(X):=(\tau_{\le n}\tau_{\ge n}X)[n],$$
an object of the heart $\mathcal C=\mathcal T^{\le0}\cap\mathcal T^{\ge0}$ ([[lem-t-cohomology-is-additive-shift-compatible-and-detects-amplitude]]). The **amplitude** of $X$ is the set of $n$ with $H^n_t(X)\not\cong0$; it is *contained in* an interval $[a,b]$ when $H^n_t(X)=0$ for every $n\notin[a,b]$. Existence of the truncation triangle is the t-structure axiom itself, applied to $X[n]$ and shifted; the essential uniqueness of that triangle, the functoriality of the truncations and all algebraic properties of $\tau_{\le n}$, $\tau_{\ge n}$ and $H^n_t$ are proved in the two immediately following lemmas.

and let $\operatorname{Aut}(x)$ act on this finite set by precomposition. For $f\in[x,z]_y$, write

\operatorname{Aut}(f/z):=\{a\in\operatorname{Aut}(x): f\circ a=f\}.

g^z_{x,y} = \sum_{[f]\in[x,z]_y/\operatorname{Aut}(x)} \frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}(f/z)|} \prod_{i>0}|\operatorname{Ext}^{-i}(x,z)|^{(-1)^i} |\operatorname{Ext}^{-i}(x,x)|^{(-1)^{i+1}}

and equivalently

All products are finite because perfect modules have finite total Ext.

[[def-hall-finitary-abelian-category]], and let $R$ be a commutative ring
with unit. Define the free $R$-module

where $[M]$ is a basis symbol for the isomorphism class of $M$. For objects $N,L$, let
$$\operatorname{Mon}_{\mathcal A}(N,L):=\{f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(N,L): f\text{ is monic}\}.$$

Fix a finite field $k=\mathbb F_q$ ([[def-finite-field-and-its-order]]). Its field operations make it a commutative ring with unit by [[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]]; this is the base ring for all DGA and dg-module structures below. A **small $k$-linear dg-category** $\mathcal T$ has a set of objects, a cochain complex $\mathcal T(a,b)$ of $k$-vector spaces for every ordered pair, closed degree-zero identity maps, and associative degree-zero composition chain maps
$$ \mathcal T(b,c)\otimes_k\mathcal T(a,b)\longrightarrow\mathcal T(a,c). $$
The cohomological grading and differential follow [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. For cochain complexes U,V use the direct-sum total tensor complex
$$ (U\otimes_k V)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}U^p\otimes_k V^q,\qquad d_{U\otimes V}(f\otimes g)=d_U f\otimes g+(-1)^p f\otimes d_Vg \quad(f\in U^p,\ g\in V^q). $$
The formula is k-balanced and additive because the two differentials are k-linear; extend it linearly from homogeneous tensors. It has degree $+1$ and squares to zero: on $f\otimes g$ its two mixed terms have coefficients $(-1)^{p+1}$ and $(-1)^p$, which cancel, and the remaining terms contain $d_U^2f$ or $d_V^2g$. Every element has finite support in the displayed direct sum, so this construction imposes no boundedness on U,V.

Writing $fg=f\circ g$ for $f\in\mathcal T(b,c)^p$ and $g\in\mathcal T(a,b)^q$, the requirement that composition commute with these differentials says exactly
$$ d(fg)=(df)g+(-1)^p f(dg). $$
Thus each endomorphism complex is a cohomological DGA in the sense of [[def-differential-graded-algebra]]: its multiplication is associative, unital and k-bilinear by the dg-category axioms, the scalar map is $\lambda\mapsto\lambda1_a$ and is central since $(\lambda1_a)f=\lambda f=f(\lambda1_a)$, and the displayed formula is precisely the DGA Leibniz rule. The identity has degree zero and is closed, as required above.

The dg-category is **locally finite** when, for every $a,b$, the graded vector space $\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i(\mathcal T(a,b))$ is finite-dimensional. Thus the cohomology is finite-dimensional and vanishes outside a finite set of degrees; no uniform bound over all pairs is assumed.

$$ M(b)\otimes_k\mathcal T(a,b)\longrightarrow M(a),\qquad m\otimes f\longmapsto mf, $$
with the tensor differential just fixed. For homogeneous $m\in M(b)^q$ and $f\in\mathcal T(a,b)^p$, its chain-map identity is
$$ d_M(mf)=d_M(m)f+(-1)^q m\,d_{\mathcal T}(f). $$
The actions are unital and compatible with composition. In particular, on each endomorphism algebra $\mathcal T(a,a)$ they give exactly the right differential graded module structure of [[def-differential-graded-module]], with the sign determined by the degree of m, not of f. This means it is obtained from finitely many representables by finite direct sums, shifts, cones, and direct summands. For perfect modules set
$$ \operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathcal T}(x,y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D(\mathcal T)}(x,y[i]). $$

$q:E\twoheadrightarrow M$ and every morphism $f:P\to M$, there exists a

Let $\mathcal T$ be a locally finite dg-enhancement over $\mathbb F_q$, and let $\mathcal D=\operatorname{Perf}(\mathcal T)$. Suppose $\mathcal D$ has a bounded t-structure whose heart $\mathcal A$ is a small finitary hereditary abelian category, and suppose the inclusion induces an exact equivalence $D^b(\mathcal A)\simeq\mathcal D$ under which short exact sequences in $\mathcal A$ correspond to distinguished triangles with all three terms in the heart. Here **hereditary** means cohomological dimension at most one: $\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal A)}(M,N[i])=0$ for all $M,N\in\mathcal A$ and $i>1$.

The untwisted Hall product [[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]] uses the convention that $[M]*_{\mathcal A}[N]$ counts subobjects isomorphic to $N$ with quotient $M$. With this convention, the basis map
$$
\Phi:H_{\mathcal A,\mathbb Q}\longrightarrow\mathcal{DH}(\mathcal T), \qquad [M]\longmapsto\chi_M
$$
is an injective algebra anti-homomorphism:
$$
\Phi([M]*_{\mathcal A}[N])=\Phi([N])*_{\mathcal{DH}}\Phi([M]).
$$
Equivalently, it is an algebra embedding $H_{\mathcal A,\mathbb Q}^{\mathrm{op}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{DH}(\mathcal T)$. Its image is the subalgebra spanned by the characteristic functions of heart objects.

derivations.claim: Kernels and cokernels of representation morphisms are formed vertexwise and inherit the arrow map; the coimage-to-image map is an isomorphism at both vertices, so $\mathcal A$ is abelian. Replacing each vertex space by $k^m$ gives a set-sized equivalent category of matrices $k^m\to k^n$. A morphism is a pair of matrices satisfying the arrow-commuting equation, hence each Hom set is finite.

The representations $P_1=(k\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}k)$ and $P_2=(0\to k)$ are projective because $\operatorname{Hom}(P_1,V)\cong V_1$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(P_2,V)\cong V_2$, and vertex evaluation preserves epimorphisms. For $V=(V_1\xrightarrow{a}V_2)$, the sequence $0\to P_2\otimes_kV_1\xrightarrow{\iota}(P_1\otimes_kV_1)\oplus(P_2\otimes_kV_2)\xrightarrow{\pi}V\to0$ has $\pi_1=\mathrm{id}_{V_1}$, $\pi_2(u,v)=a(u)+v$, and $\iota_2(u)=(u,-a(u))$ with $\iota_1=0$. Its vertexwise kernel equals the image of $\iota$, so this is a length-one projective resolution. The resulting two-term projective complex $P$ is homotopically projective: for any acyclic cochain complex $C$ and chain map $f:P\to C$, projectivity lifts $f^0:P^0\to Z^0(C)$ through $d_C^{-1}:C^{-1}\twoheadrightarrow Z^0(C)$ to $h^0$; then $u^{-1}=f^{-1}-h^0d_P^{-1}$ lands in $Z^{-1}(C)$, and projectivity lifts it through $d_C^{-2}$ to $h^{-1}$. The equations $f^0=d_C^{-1}h^0$ and $f^{-1}=d_C^{-2}h^{-1}+h^0d_P^{-1}$ give a null-homotopy; only two lifts are used. By [F3], $\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal A)}(V,W[i])$ is computed by $\operatorname{Hom}(P,W[i])$, which vanishes for $i>1$. Thus the canonical heart is hereditary in the cohomological-dimension sense of [F4].

A middle representation has dimension vector $(1,1)$ and is a scalar map $\lambda:k\to k$. Isomorphisms act by $(g_1,g_2)\cdot\lambda=g_2\lambda g_1^{-1}$ with $g_1,g_2\in k^\times$. The zero scalar is one orbit, and all nonzero scalars form one orbit: for $\lambda,\mu\ne0$, $g_1=1$ and $g_2=\mu\lambda^{-1}$ send $\lambda$ to $\mu$. Hence the only middle classes are $S_1\oplus S_2$ and $P_1$.

A short exact sequence with fixed endpoints has middle dimension vector equal to the sum of their dimension vectors. There are finitely many arrow matrices for that dimension vector and finitely many injection and quotient matrices, so there are finitely many short exact sequences; their Yoneda classes are a quotient of this finite set. Thus $\mathcal A$ is small finitary as required by [F1].

In either middle representation the only subrepresentation isomorphic to $S_2$ has vertex spaces $(0,k)$, and its quotient is $S_1$. The short exact sequence fixes dimension vector $(1,1)$, so no other middle classes contribute. Thus $g^{S_1\oplus S_2}_{S_1,S_2}=1$ and $g^{P_1}_{S_1,S_2}=1$.

By steps 1.1–1.2 and [A1], $\mathcal A$ satisfies the finitary, hereditary, boundedness and exact-heart hypotheses of [F4]. Applying [F4] to the two coefficients from step 2.2 gives the displayed derived Hall product; the order is the opposite-heart order, as stated.
